claim: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) is a chronic metabolic disorder characterized by elevated blood glucose levels and increased risk of numerous serious and life-threatening complications.
source: Type 2 diabetes (T2D), a chronic metabolic disorder characterized by elevated blood glucose levels and increased risk of numerous serious and life-threatening complications, constitutes one of the biggest health problems in the world (Diamond, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Diamond, 2003

claim: The age-standardized global prevalence of type 2 diabetes was approximately 6.0% in men and 5.0% in women in 2019.
source: According to Global Burden of Disease (GBD) data, the age-standardized global prevalence of type 2 diabetes was approximately 6.0% in men and 5.0% in women in 2019 (Tinajero and Malik, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tinajero and Malik, 2021, referencing GBD data

claim: Type 2 diabetes accounts for more than 100 billion dollars of healthcare costs annually in the United States.
source: It accounts for more than 100 billion dollars of healthcare costs annually in the United States (Diamond, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Diamond, 2003

claim: The chronic comorbidities of T2D could develop gradually and could lead to serious damage to the heart, blood vessels, kidneys, eyes, and feet.
source: The chronic comorbidities of T2D could develop gradually, and could lead to serious damage to the heart, blood vessels, kidneys, eyes, and feet (Teck, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Teck, 2022

claim: Skeletal health could be influenced by T2D.
source: Other organ systems such as skeletal health could also be influenced by T2D (Lei and Kindler, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lei and Kindler, 2022

claim: Osteoporosis is a common musculoskeletal disease characterized by low bone mass and disruption of bone microarchitecture, leading to an increased risk of fracture.
source: Osteoporosis is a common musculoskeletal disease characterized by low bone mass and disruption of bone microarchitecture, leading to an increased risk of fracture.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about osteoporosis

claim: Bone mass and fracture could be influenced by many modifiable or non-modifiable factors such as body weight, sleep behavior, inflammatory disease, birth weight, and genetic factors.
source: Our previous studies have suggested that bone mass and fracture could be influenced by many modifiable or non-modifiable factors (Zhu and Zheng, 2021), such as body weight (Zhu et al., 2022), sleep behavior (Qian et al., 2021), inflammatory disease (Xia et al., 2020), birth weight (Xia et al., 2022), and genetic factors (Zhu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies

claim: T2D patients would have higher BMD and higher fracture risk than individuals without T2D, which is called the 'diabetic bone paradox'.
source: T2D is also considered to be a major factor that could affect bone health, it seems that T2D patients would have higher BMD and higher fracture risk than individuals without T2D (Khosla et al., 2021). This is the so-called 'diabetic bone paradox' (Botella Martínez et al., 2016; Romero-Díaz et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Khosla et al., 2021; Botella Martínez et al., 2016; Romero-Díaz et al., 2021

claim: In an Italian nationwide study of 59,950 women of whom 5.2% had diabetes, diabetes was associated with any fracture (OR 1.3, 95% CI 1.1–1.4).
source: For example, in an Italian nationwide study of 59,950 women of whom 5.2% had diabetes (predominantly type 2 diabetes), noted an association between diabetes and any fracture (OR 1.3, 95% CI 1.1–1.4, and OR 1.3, 95% CI 1.2–1.5, for vertebral or hip fractures and non-vertebral, non-hip fractures, respectively) (Adami et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Adami et al., 2020, reporting observational study data

claim: The prevalence of vertebral or hip fracture was higher in participants with diabetes but without obesity (OR 1.9, 95% CI 1.7–2.1) than in patients with obesity and diabetes (OR 1.5, 95% CI 1.3–1.8).
source: Interestingly, the prevalence of vertebral or hip fracture was higher in participants with diabetes but without obesity (OR 1.9, 95% CI 1.7–2.1) than in patients with obesity and diabetes (OR 1.5, 95% CI 1.3–1.8), suggesting that obesity might be partially protective against vertebral or hip fractures in type 2 diabetes (Adami et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Adami et al., 2020, reporting observational study data

claim: Obesity might be partially protective against vertebral or hip fractures in type 2 diabetes.
source: Interestingly, the prevalence of vertebral or hip fracture was higher in participants with diabetes but without obesity (OR 1.9, 95% CI 1.7–2.1) than in patients with obesity and diabetes (OR 1.5, 95% CI 1.3–1.8), suggesting that obesity might be partially protective against vertebral or hip fractures in type 2 diabetes (Adami et al., 2020).
evidence: Inference drawn from observational data cited from Adami et al., 2020

claim: A UK primary care records study found no evidence to suggest a higher risk of fracture in type 2 diabetes patients.
source: However, a recent comparative cohort analysis using routinely collected UK primary care records data from the Health Improvement Network (including 174,244 individuals with incident type 2 diabetes and 747,290 without diabetes) found no evidence to suggest a higher risk of fracture in type 2 diabetes patients, specifically, the risk of having at least one fracture was estimated to be 6% lower for females and 3% lower for males in the type 2 diabetes cohort than for females and males without diabetes (Davie et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Davie et al., 2021, reporting observational study data

claim: The risk of having at least one fracture was estimated to be 6% lower for females and 3% lower for males in the type 2 diabetes cohort than for those without diabetes.
source: However, a recent comparative cohort analysis using routinely collected UK primary care records data from the Health Improvement Network (including 174,244 individuals with incident type 2 diabetes and 747,290 without diabetes) found no evidence to suggest a higher risk of fracture in type 2 diabetes patients, specifically, the risk of having at least one fracture was estimated to be 6% lower for females and 3% lower for males in the type 2 diabetes cohort than for females and males without diabetes (Davie et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Davie et al., 2021, reporting observational study data

claim: Lower fracture risk was observed in type 2 diabetes patients compared to those without the disease in the age group greater than 85 years.
source: Lower fracture risk was also observed in the type 2 diabetes patients compared to those without the disease in the age group greater than 85 years (Davie et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Davie et al., 2021, reporting observational study data

claim: Type 2 diabetes could only explain less than 0.1% of the fracture risk.
source: Another large-scale cohort study showed that type 2 diabetes could only explain less than 0.1% of the fracture risk (Axelsson et al., 2023), and if the T2D patients with risk factors (such as low BMI, long diabetes duration, insulin treatment, and low physical activity) were excluded, T2D patients would have lower fracture risk than their matched controls (Axelsson et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Axelsson et al., 2023, reporting observational study data

claim: If T2D patients with risk factors (such as low BMI, long diabetes duration, insulin treatment, and low physical activity) were excluded, T2D patients would have lower fracture risk than their matched controls.
source: Another large-scale cohort study showed that type 2 diabetes could only explain less than 0.1% of the fracture risk (Axelsson et al., 2023), and if the T2D patients with risk factors (such as low BMI, long diabetes duration, insulin treatment, and low physical activity) were excluded, T2D patients would have lower fracture risk than their matched controls (Axelsson et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Axelsson et al., 2023, reporting observational study data

claim: Femoral neck BMD T score and FRAX score were both associated with fracture risk in individuals with type 2 diabetes.
source: In a prospective study to examine the relationship between BMD and fracture in older adults with type 2 diabetes, it was reported that femoral neck BMD T score and FRAX score were both associated with fracture risk in individuals with type 2 diabetes, suggesting that BMD is still a useful clinical predictor for the evaluation of fracture risk in type 2 diabetes patients (Schwartz et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schwartz et al., 2011, reporting observational study data

claim: BMD is still a useful clinical predictor for the evaluation of fracture risk in type 2 diabetes patients.
source: In a prospective study to examine the relationship between BMD and fracture in older adults with type 2 diabetes, it was reported that femoral neck BMD T score and FRAX score were both associated with fracture risk in individuals with type 2 diabetes, suggesting that BMD is still a useful clinical predictor for the evaluation of fracture risk in type 2 diabetes patients (Schwartz et al., 2011).
evidence: Inference drawn from observational data cited from Schwartz et al., 2011

claim: The wGRS of 404 SNPs were strongly associated with type 2 diabetes in UK Biobank data (OR = 1.6, p<2.0 × 10–16).
source: The wGRS of the 404 SNPs were strongly associated with type 2 diabetes in UK Biobank data (OR = 1.6, p<2.0 × 10–16), suggesting that the instruments were powerful for the MR analysis.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of UK Biobank data

claim: The genetically determined type 2 diabetes was associated with a lower risk of fracture (OR = 0.982, 95%CI = 0.975–0.989, p=0.006) in wGRS analysis.
source: When we regressed the observed fracture on the wGRS, we found that the genetically determined type 2 diabetes was associated with a lower risk of fracture (OR = 0.982, 95%CI = 0.975–0.989, p=0.006) (adjusting for reference age, sex, BMI, physical activity, fall history, HbA1c, and medication treatments) (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by wGRS regression analysis in UK Biobank data, shown in Figure 2A

claim: There was a trend of protective association between T2D wGRS and weight-bearing bones fracture (OR = 0.9772, 95%CI = 0.9552–0.9997, p=0.04737).
source: When we classified the fracture sites into weight-bearing bones (neck, vertebrae, pelvic, femur, tibia) and other bones, it indicated that there was a trend of protective association between T2D wGRS and weight-bearing bones fracture (OR = 0.9772, 95%CI = 0.9552–0.9997, p=0.04737, N of fracture = 8992, N of non-fracture=265,262), and other bones fracture (OR = 0.9838, 95%CI = 0.9688–0.9991, p=0.0386, N of fracture = 20,317, N of non-fracture=265,262) (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by wGRS regression analysis in UK Biobank data, shown in Figure 2A

claim: There was a trend of protective association between T2D wGRS and other bones fracture (OR = 0.9838, 95%CI = 0.9688–0.9991, p=0.0386).
source: When we classified the fracture sites into weight-bearing bones (neck, vertebrae, pelvic, femur, tibia) and other bones, it indicated that there was a trend of protective association between T2D wGRS and weight-bearing bones fracture (OR = 0.9772, 95%CI = 0.9552–0.9997, p=0.04737, N of fracture = 8992, N of non-fracture=265,262), and other bones fracture (OR = 0.9838, 95%CI = 0.9688–0.9991, p=0.0386, N of fracture = 20,317, N of non-fracture=265,262) (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by wGRS regression analysis in UK Biobank data, shown in Figure 2A

claim: No significant sex interactions were identified for fracture risk with T2D wGRS (p=0.5576).
source: We further estimated the effect of sex interaction on fracture risk with T2D wGRS × sex interaction term in the regression model, and no significant interactions were identified for fracture risk (p=0.5576).
evidence: Supported by interaction analysis in UK Biobank data

claim: The genetically determined type 2 diabetes was associated with higher BMD in pooled samples.
source: Meanwhile, the genetically determined type 2 diabetes was associated with higher BMD in pooled samples (Figure 2B) and in both males and females (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by wGRS regression analysis in UK Biobank data, shown in Figure 2B

claim: The genetically determined type 2 diabetes was associated with higher BMD in both males and females.
source: Meanwhile, the genetically determined type 2 diabetes was associated with higher BMD in pooled samples (Figure 2B) and in both males and females (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by wGRS regression analysis in UK Biobank data, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: The inverse variance weighting (IVW) method showed a causal effect of genetically predicted T2D on low fracture risk (OR = 0.965, 95%CI = 0.943–0.988, p=0.003).
source: The inverse variance weighting (IVW) method showed a causal effect of genetically predicted T2D on low fracture risk (OR = 0.965, 95%CI = 0.943–0.988, p=0.003) (Figure 2A) using 298 SNPs as the instruments (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Supported by two-sample MR analysis using IVW method, shown in Figure 2A

claim: The causal relationship between T2D and fracture was significant in the simple median test (OR = 0.967, 95%CI = 0.936–0.997, p=0.033).
source: This causal relationship was also significant in the simple median test (OR = 0.967, 95%CI = 0.936–0.997, p=0.033) (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by two-sample MR analysis using simple median method, shown in Figure 2A

claim: There was heterogeneity in IVW results (Q' p<0.05).
source: There was heterogeneity in IVW results (Q' p<0.05), when we excluded pleiotropic variants using restrictive MR pleiotropy residual sum and outlier test (MR-PRESSO) method, the causal association was still detected between T2D and fracture (OR = 0.967, 95%CI = 0.945–0.989, p=0.004) (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by heterogeneity test in two-sample MR analysis

claim: After excluding pleiotropic variants using MR-PRESSO method, the causal association was still detected between T2D and fracture (OR = 0.967, 95%CI = 0.945–0.989, p=0.004).
source: There was heterogeneity in IVW results (Q' p<0.05), when we excluded pleiotropic variants using restrictive MR pleiotropy residual sum and outlier test (MR-PRESSO) method, the causal association was still detected between T2D and fracture (OR = 0.967, 95%CI = 0.945–0.989, p=0.004) (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by two-sample MR analysis using MR-PRESSO method, shown in Figure 2A

claim: The MR-egger regression suggested an inverse association between T2D and fracture (OR = 0.9666, 95%CI = 0.9497–0.9828, p=0.0002).
source: Moreover, the MR-egger regression also suggested an inverse association between T2D and fracture (OR = 0.9666, 95%CI = 0.9497–0.9828, p=0.0002) (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by two-sample MR analysis using MR-egger method, shown in Figure 2C

claim: Two of 298 lead SNPs (including rs4580892 near RSPO3) of T2D remained as potential regions which would also have effect on fracture after FDR correction.
source: The individual effect of the SNPs for T2D on fracture was corrected by the false discovery rate (<0.05) (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995), two of 298 lead SNPs (including rs4580892 near RSPO3) of T2D remained as potential regions which would also have effect on fracture (Figure 2C and Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Supported by FDR-corrected analysis of individual SNP effects, shown in Figure 2C

claim: T2D had a direct effect on decreased fracture risk adjusted for BMI (OR = 0.974, 95%CI = 0.953–0.995, p=0.017).
source: We also performed multivariable MR analysis to test the effect of T2D on fracture risk-adjusted for confounding factors. We found that T2D had a direct effect on decreased fracture risk adjusted for BMI (OR = 0.974, 95%CI = 0.953–0.995, p=0.017), and BMI mediated 9.03% of the protective effect (Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: Supported by multivariable MR analysis

claim: BMI mediated 9.03% of the protective effect of T2D on fracture risk in multivariable MR analysis.
source: We also performed multivariable MR analysis to test the effect of T2D on fracture risk-adjusted for confounding factors. We found that T2D had a direct effect on decreased fracture risk adjusted for BMI (OR = 0.974, 95%CI = 0.953–0.995, p=0.017), and BMI mediated 9.03% of the protective effect (Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: Supported by multivariable MR analysis with mediation calculation

claim: IVW showed a causal association between type 2 diabetes and BMD (β=0.041, 95%CI = 0.027–0.054, p=8.14 × 10–9).
source: Similarly, with BMD GWAS summary data (Morris et al., 2019), IVW (β=0.041, 95%CI = 0.027–0.054, p=8.14 × 10–9), simple median (β=0.028, 95%CI = 0.020–0.036, p=6.59 × 10–13), and MR-PRESSO (β=0.029, 95%CI = 0.022–0.036, p=1.14 × 10–14) all showed a causal association between type 2 diabetes and BMD (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: Supported by two-sample MR analysis using IVW method, shown in Figure 2B

claim: Simple median showed a causal association between type 2 diabetes and BMD (β=0.028, 95%CI = 0.020–0.036, p=6.59 × 10–13).
source: Similarly, with BMD GWAS summary data (Morris et al., 2019), IVW (β=0.041, 95%CI = 0.027–0.054, p=8.14 × 10–9), simple median (β=0.028, 95%CI = 0.020–0.036, p=6.59 × 10–13), and MR-PRESSO (β=0.029, 95%CI = 0.022–0.036, p=1.14 × 10–14) all showed a causal association between type 2 diabetes and BMD (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: Supported by two-sample MR analysis using simple median method, shown in Figure 2B

claim: MR-PRESSO showed a causal association between type 2 diabetes and BMD (β=0.029, 95%CI = 0.022–0.036, p=1.14 × 10–14).
source: Similarly, with BMD GWAS summary data (Morris et al., 2019), IVW (β=0.041, 95%CI = 0.027–0.054, p=8.14 × 10–9), simple median (β=0.028, 95%CI = 0.020–0.036, p=6.59 × 10–13), and MR-PRESSO (β=0.029, 95%CI = 0.022–0.036, p=1.14 × 10–14) all showed a causal association between type 2 diabetes and BMD (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: Supported by two-sample MR analysis using MR-PRESSO method, shown in Figure 2B

claim: T2D showed a direct effect on increased BMD after adjusting for BMI (β=0.042, 95%CI = 0.026–0.057, p=1.92 × 10–7).
source: The multivariable MR analysis suggested that T2D also showed a direct effect on increased BMD after adjusting for BMI (β=0.042, 95%CI = 0.026–0.057, p=1.92 × 10–7) (Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: Supported by multivariable MR analysis

claim: The genetic correlation between type 2 diabetes and fracture was not significant, but with inverse direction (rg = −0.0114).
source: It is found that the genetic correlation between type 2 diabetes and fracture was not significant, but with inverse direction (rg = −0.0114) (Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: Supported by LDSC analysis

claim: Type 2 diabetes and fracture exhibited polygenic overlap, sharing 428 causal variants.
source: As represented in Venn diagrams of shared and unique polygenic components (Figure 3a), the MiXeR analysis suggested that type 2 diabetes and fracture exhibited polygenic overlap, sharing 428 causal variants, in other words, 18% of variants (428 of 2370) associated with type 2 diabetes might contribute to the risk of fracture (Dice coefficient = 25.25%), and genetic correlation was observed (rg = –0.086) (Figure 3A and Supplementary file 1f).
evidence: Supported by MiXeR analysis, shown in Figure 3A

claim: 18% of variants (428 of 2370) associated with type 2 diabetes might contribute to the risk of fracture.
source: As represented in Venn diagrams of shared and unique polygenic components (Figure 3a), the MiXeR analysis suggested that type 2 diabetes and fracture exhibited polygenic overlap, sharing 428 causal variants, in other words, 18% of variants (428 of 2370) associated with type 2 diabetes might contribute to the risk of fracture (Dice coefficient = 25.25%), and genetic correlation was observed (rg = –0.086) (Figure 3A and Supplementary file 1f).
evidence: Supported by MiXeR analysis, shown in Figure 3A

claim: Only 39% of shared variants between type 2 diabetes and fracture showed a concordant direction of the association.
source: Only 39% of shared variants between type 2 diabetes and fracture showed a concordant direction of the association, and the correlation of effect sizes within the shared polygenic component was negative (rho_β = −0.336) (Supplementary file 1f).
evidence: Supported by MiXeR analysis

claim: The correlation of effect sizes within the shared polygenic component between T2D and fracture was negative (rho_β = −0.336).
source: Only 39% of shared variants between type 2 diabetes and fracture showed a concordant direction of the association, and the correlation of effect sizes within the shared polygenic component was negative (rho_β = −0.336) (Supplementary file 1f).
evidence: Supported by MiXeR analysis

claim: The conjFDR analysis identified 10 genomic loci shared between type 2 diabetes and fracture.
source: The conjunctional false discovery rate (conjFDR) analysis identified 10 genomic loci shared between type 2 diabetes and fracture (Figure 3C and Supplementary file 1g), with the top SNP rs4580892 in the intron of gene RSPO3 (conjFDR = 1.45E-05).
evidence: Supported by conjFDR analysis, shown in Figure 3C

claim: The top SNP shared between type 2 diabetes and fracture is rs4580892 in the intron of gene RSPO3 (conjFDR = 1.45E-05).
source: The conjunctional false discovery rate (conjFDR) analysis identified 10 genomic loci shared between type 2 diabetes and fracture (Figure 3C and Supplementary file 1g), with the top SNP rs4580892 in the intron of gene RSPO3 (conjFDR = 1.45E-05).
evidence: Supported by conjFDR analysis, shown in Figure 3C

claim: 7 of 10 shared loci had an inverse direction of effect between type 2 diabetes and fracture.
source: The shared loci showed mixed directions of allelic associations, with 7 of 10 shared loci had an inverse direction of effect between type 2 diabetes and fracture (Supplementary file 1g).
evidence: Supported by conjFDR analysis results

claim: rs4580892_T allele was associated with increased type 2 diabetes risk (OR = 1.041227, p=8.46 × 10–9).
source: The top SNP rs4580892 had an inverse direction of effect between type 2 diabetes and fracture, where rs4580892_T allele was associated with increased type 2 diabetes risk (OR = 1.041227, p=8.46 × 10–9) (Figure 4A) and decreased fracture risk (OR = 0.944, p=3.68 × 10–10) (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by GWAS summary data analysis, shown in Figure 4A

claim: rs4580892_T allele was associated with decreased fracture risk (OR = 0.944, p=3.68 × 10–10).
source: The top SNP rs4580892 had an inverse direction of effect between type 2 diabetes and fracture, where rs4580892_T allele was associated with increased type 2 diabetes risk (OR = 1.041227, p=8.46 × 10–9) (Figure 4A) and decreased fracture risk (OR = 0.944, p=3.68 × 10–10) (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by GWAS summary data analysis, shown in Figure 4B

claim: Higher expression of RSPO3 in adipose subcutaneous would be associated with increased the risk of type 2 diabetes (OR = 1.102, 95%CI = 1.031–1.179, p=0.004).
source: By applying the SMR method (Zhu et al., 2016), we found that the higher expression of RSPO3 (ENSG00000146374) in adipose subcutaneous would be associated with increased the risk of type 2 diabetes (OR = 1.102, 95%CI = 1.031–1.179, p=0.004), but decreased the risk of fracture (OR = 0.695, 95%CI = 0.566–0.854, p=0.0005) (Figure 4C and Supplementary file 1h).
evidence: Supported by SMR analysis, shown in Figure 4C

claim: Higher expression of RSPO3 in adipose subcutaneous would be associated with decreased the risk of fracture (OR = 0.695, 95%CI = 0.566–0.854, p=0.0005).
source: By applying the SMR method (Zhu et al., 2016), we found that the higher expression of RSPO3 (ENSG00000146374) in adipose subcutaneous would be associated with increased the risk of type 2 diabetes (OR = 1.102, 95%CI = 1.031–1.179, p=0.004), but decreased the risk of fracture (OR = 0.695, 95%CI = 0.566–0.854, p=0.0005) (Figure 4C and Supplementary file 1h).
evidence: Supported by SMR analysis, shown in Figure 4C

claim: Higher expression of RSPO3 in adipose subcutaneous was associated with higher waist circumference (β=0.090, 95%CI = 0.029–0.151, p=0.004).
source: Interestingly, in adipose subcutaneous, higher expression of RSPO3 was associated with higher waist circumference (β=0.090, 95%CI = 0.029–0.151, p=0.004) and higher waist-hip ratio (β=0.204, 95%CI = 0.095–0.313, p=0.0002) (Figure 4D and Supplementary file 1h).
evidence: Supported by SMR analysis, shown in Figure 4D

claim: Higher expression of RSPO3 in adipose subcutaneous was associated with higher waist-hip ratio (β=0.204, 95%CI = 0.095–0.313, p=0.0002).
source: Interestingly, in adipose subcutaneous, higher expression of RSPO3 was associated with higher waist circumference (β=0.090, 95%CI = 0.029–0.151, p=0.004) and higher waist-hip ratio (β=0.204, 95%CI = 0.095–0.313, p=0.0002) (Figure 4D and Supplementary file 1h).
evidence: Supported by SMR analysis, shown in Figure 4D

claim: Higher expression of RSPO3 was associated with higher MRI-derived visceral adipose (β=0.199, 95%CI = 0.103–0.294, p=4.36 × 10–5).
source: Meanwhile, higher expression of RSPO3 was associated with higher MRI-derived visceral adipose (β=0.199, 95%CI = 0.103–0.294, p=4.36 × 10–5) (Figure 4D and Supplementary file 1h).
evidence: Supported by SMR analysis, shown in Figure 4D

claim: Increased circulating RSPO3 was strongly associated with increased risk of type 2 diabetes (OR = 1.24, 95%CI = 1.16–1.34, p=7.86 × 10−9).
source: The MR analyses indicated that increased circulating RSPO3 was strongly associated with increased risk of type 2 diabetes (OR = 1.24, 95%CI = 1.16–1.34, p=7.86  ×  10−9), but reduced fracture risk (OR = 0.73, 95%CI = 0.66–0.81, p=4.1  ×  10−10) (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by MR analysis using pQTL data, shown in Figure 4E

claim: Increased circulating RSPO3 was associated with reduced fracture risk (OR = 0.73, 95%CI = 0.66–0.81, p=4.1 × 10−10).
source: The MR analyses indicated that increased circulating RSPO3 was strongly associated with increased risk of type 2 diabetes (OR = 1.24, 95%CI = 1.16–1.34, p=7.86  ×  10−9), but reduced fracture risk (OR = 0.73, 95%CI = 0.66–0.81, p=4.1  ×  10−10) (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by MR analysis using pQTL data, shown in Figure 4E

claim: Type 2 diabetes showed a significant positive genetic correlation with BMD (rg = 0.0923, p=2.50 × 10–6).
source: Not surprisingly, type 2 diabetes showed a significant positive genetic correlation with BMD (rg = 0.0923, p=2.50 × 10–6) (Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: Supported by LDSC analysis

claim: 29% of variants (691 of 2370) associated with type 2 diabetes might contribute to BMD (Dice coefficient = 33.67%).
source: The MiXeR analysis suggested that 29% of variants (691 of 2370) associated with type 2 diabetes might contribute to BMD (Dice coefficient = 33.67%) (Figure 3D and Supplementary file 1f).
evidence: Supported by MiXeR analysis, shown in Figure 3D

claim: The conjFDR analysis identified 661 genomic loci shared between type 2 diabetes and BMD.
source: The leftward deflected from the expected null line in the QQ plot suggested the existence of a polygenic overlap between type 2 diabetes and BMD (Figure 3E). and the conjFDR analysis identified 661 genomic loci shared between type 2 diabetes and BMD, and 449 of 661 loci (68%) had concordant associations between type 2 diabetes and BMD (Figure 3F and Supplementary file 1i).
evidence: Supported by conjFDR analysis, shown in Figure 3F

claim: 449 of 661 loci (68%) had concordant associations between type 2 diabetes and BMD.
source: The leftward deflected from the expected null line in the QQ plot suggested the existence of a polygenic overlap between type 2 diabetes and BMD (Figure 3E). and the conjFDR analysis identified 661 genomic loci shared between type 2 diabetes and BMD, and 449 of 661 loci (68%) had concordant associations between type 2 diabetes and BMD (Figure 3F and Supplementary file 1i).
evidence: Supported by conjFDR analysis, shown in Figure 3F

claim: Within the 352,879 UK Biobank participants, 13,817 (3.92%) developed type 2 diabetes during 2006 and 2015.
source: Within the 352,879 UK Biobank participants (Figure 1), 13,817 (3.92%) developed type 2 diabetes during 2006 and 2015, with the mean duration of type 2 diabetes 8.34 years (Supplementary file 1j).
evidence: Supported by UK Biobank observational data

claim: The mean duration of type 2 diabetes was 8.34 years in the UK Biobank cohort.
source: Within the 352,879 UK Biobank participants (Figure 1), 13,817 (3.92%) developed type 2 diabetes during 2006 and 2015, with the mean duration of type 2 diabetes 8.34 years (Supplementary file 1j).
evidence: Supported by UK Biobank observational data

claim: Participants with type 2 diabetes were older (63.20 vs 60.55, p<2.2 × 10−16) compared to those without diabetes.
source: Compared to those without diabetes, the participants with type 2 diabetes were older (63.20 vs 60.55, p<2.2 × 10−16), and more likely to be men and smokers, and had a higher BMI (32.07 vs 27.08, p<2.2 × 10−16) (Supplementary file 1j).
evidence: Supported by UK Biobank observational data

claim: Participants with type 2 diabetes had a higher BMI (32.07 vs 27.08, p<2.2 × 10−16) compared to those without diabetes.
source: Compared to those without diabetes, the participants with type 2 diabetes were older (63.20 vs 60.55, p<2.2 × 10−16), and more likely to be men and smokers, and had a higher BMI (32.07 vs 27.08, p<2.2 × 10−16) (Supplementary file 1j).
evidence: Supported by UK Biobank observational data

claim: 16,147 (4.6%) participants had fractures within the 352,879 UK Biobank participants.
source: We identified 16,147 (4.6%) participants with fractures within the 352,879 UK Biobank participants (Supplementary file 1j).
evidence: Supported by UK Biobank observational data

claim: Type 2 diabetes patients had a higher risk of fracture (HR = 1.527, 95% CI 1.385–1.685, p<2 × 10−16) after adjusting for reference age, sex, BMI, physical activity, HbA1c, medication treatments, and fall history.
source: Although we found that genetically predicted type 2 diabetes might not be associated with risk of fracture, we observed a higher risk of fracture in the type 2 diabetes patients in the Cox proportional hazards regression after adjusting for the reference age, sex, BMI, physical activity, HbA1c, medication treatments, and fall history (Model 0) (HR = 1.527, 95% CI 1.385–1.685, p<2 × 10−16) (Figure 5A and Supplementary file 1k).
evidence: Supported by Cox regression analysis in UK Biobank, shown in Figure 5A

claim: BMI mediated 30.2% of the intermediary effect between type 2 diabetes and fracture.
source: And the average causal mediation effect (ACME) by BMI was protective with 30.2% of the intermediary effect, respectively (BMI: indirect effect = −0.003, p<2 × 10–16) (Supplementary file 1l).
evidence: Supported by mediation analysis in UK Biobank

claim: When additionally controlled for BMD, an increased risk of fracture in type 2 diabetes was still observed (HR = 1.574, 95% CI 1.425–1.739, p<2 × 10−16).
source: When we additionally controlled for BMD, we still observed an increased risk of fracture in type 2 diabetes (HR = 1.574, 95% CI 1.425–1.739, p<2 × 10−16) (Model 1) (Figure 5A and Supplementary file 1k).
evidence: Supported by Cox regression analysis in UK Biobank, shown in Figure 5A

claim: Type 2 diabetes was associated with weight-bearing bones fracture (HR = 1.792, 95% CI 1.555–2,065, p=8.25 × 10−16) in model 0.
source: We also classified the fracture into weight-bearing bone fractures (neck, vertebrae, pelvic, femur, tibia) and other bones fracture. Similar trends of association were observed in model 0 (weight-bearing bones: HR = 1.792, 95% CI 1.555–2,065, p=8.25 × 10−16; other bones: HR = 1.337, 95% CI 1.167–1.531, p=2.85 × 10−5) and model 1 (weight-bearing bones: HR = 1.850, 95% CI 1.602–2,136, p<2 × 10−16; other bones: HR = 1.377, 95% CI 1.199–1.580, p=5.54 × 10−6) (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by Cox regression analysis in UK Biobank, shown in Figure 5A

claim: Type 2 diabetes was associated with other bones fracture (HR = 1.337, 95% CI 1.167–1.531, p=2.85 × 10−5) in model 0.
source: We also classified the fracture into weight-bearing bone fractures (neck, vertebrae, pelvic, femur, tibia) and other bones fracture. Similar trends of association were observed in model 0 (weight-bearing bones: HR = 1.792, 95% CI 1.555–2,065, p=8.25 × 10−16; other bones: HR = 1.337, 95% CI 1.167–1.531, p=2.85 × 10−5) and model 1 (weight-bearing bones: HR = 1.850, 95% CI 1.602–2,136, p<2 × 10−16; other bones: HR = 1.377, 95% CI 1.199–1.580, p=5.54 × 10−6) (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by Cox regression analysis in UK Biobank, shown in Figure 5A

claim: Type 2 diabetes with at least two risk factors were associated with an increase in fracture risk (HR = 1.39, 95% CI 1.269–1.514, p=1.32 × 10−7).
source: We performed stratified cox regression analysis and found that type 2 diabetes with at least two risk factors were associated with an increase in fracture risk (HR = 1.39, 95% CI 1.269–1.514, p=1.32 × 10−7) (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by stratified Cox regression analysis in UK Biobank, shown in Figure 5B

claim: Including only one risk factor would attenuate the effect size of type 2 diabetes on fracture risk (HR = 1.20, 95%CI = 1.060–1.338, p=0.010).
source: It is interesting to note that including only one risk factor would attenuate the effect size of type 2 diabetes on fracture risk (HR = 1.20, 95%CI = 1.060–1.338, p=0.010).
evidence: Supported by stratified Cox regression analysis in UK Biobank

claim: The association between type 2 diabetes and fracture was not significant (p=0.452) when analyzing the type 2 diabetes without risk factors (HR = 1.08, 95% CI 0.880–1.280, n=2303).
source: Furthermore, the association between type 2 diabetes and fracture was not significant (p=0.452) when analyzing the type 2 diabetes without risk factors (HR = 1.08, 95% CI 0.880–1.280, n=2303) (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by stratified Cox regression analysis in UK Biobank, shown in Figure 5B

claim: Participants with diabetes had a significantly higher BMD than subjects without diabetes (0.57 vs 0.54, p<2.2 × 10−16).
source: We also observed that participants with diabetes, despite they were older, had a significantly higher BMD than subjects without diabetes (0.57 vs 0.54, p<2.2 × 10−16) (Supplementary file 1j).
evidence: Supported by UK Biobank observational data

claim: Type 2 diabetes was found to be associated with increased BMD (β=0.00957, p=1.35 × 10−10) after adjusting for age, sex, BMI, physical activity, fall history, HbA1c, and medication treatments.
source: In the multivariable linear regression analysis, the type 2 diabetes was found to be associated with increased BMD in the same model adjusted for age, sex, BMI, physical activity, fall history, HbA1c, and medication treatments (β=0.00957, p=1.35 × 10−10) (Figure 5CSupplementary file 1k).
evidence: Supported by linear regression analysis in UK Biobank, shown in Figure 5C

claim: The effect size of type 2 diabetes on BMD decreased when the number of risk factors increased.
source: We examined the relationship between type 2 diabetes and BMD in subgroups with varying numbers of risk factors. We observed that the effect size of type 2 diabetes on BMD decreased when the number of risk factors increased (no risk factors: in pooled β=0.023, p<2 × 10−16, in male β=0.018, p=2.09 × 10−6, in female β=0.028, p=2.97 × 10−11; one risk factor: in pooled β=0.020, p<2 × 10−16, in male β=0.015, p=1.91 × 10−7, in female β=0.0245, p=2.46 × 10−16; at least two risk factors: β=0.017, p<2 × 10−16, in male β=0.0098, p=7.74 × 10−4, in female β=0.0250, p<2 × 10−16) (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by stratified linear regression analysis in UK Biobank, shown in Figure 5C

claim: The genetically predicted T2D was associated with higher BMD and lower risk of fracture in both wGRS and two-sample MR analyses.
source: By leveraging the genetic datasets, we found that the genetically predicted T2D was associated with higher BMD and lower risk of fracture in both one-sample MR (with 404 IVs) and two-sample MR (with 298 IVs).
evidence: Supported by wGRS and two-sample MR analyses

claim: RSPO3 is a known WNT-signaling modulator.
source: RSPO3 is a known WNT-signaling modulator (Baron and Kneissel, 2013 ; Lerner and Ohlsson, 2015), which could bind to LRP5/6 to enhance the activity of osteoblast (Richards et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Baron and Kneissel, 2013; Lerner and Ohlsson, 2015

claim: RSPO3 could bind to LRP5/6 to enhance the activity of osteoblast.
source: RSPO3 is a known WNT-signaling modulator (Baron and Kneissel, 2013 ; Lerner and Ohlsson, 2015), which could bind to LRP5/6 to enhance the activity of osteoblast (Richards et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Richards et al., 2012

claim: RSPO3 is expressed in osteoprogenitor cells and osteoblasts.
source: Karin et al., demonstrated that RSPO3 is expressed in osteoprogenitor cells and osteoblasts, and that osteoblast-derived RSPO3 is the principal source of RSPO3 in bone and is an important regulator of vertebral trabecular bone mass and bone strength in adult mice (Nilsson et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nilsson et al., 2021

claim: Osteoblast-derived RSPO3 is the principal source of RSPO3 in bone and is an important regulator of vertebral trabecular bone mass and bone strength in adult mice.
source: Karin et al., demonstrated that RSPO3 is expressed in osteoprogenitor cells and osteoblasts, and that osteoblast-derived RSPO3 is the principal source of RSPO3 in bone and is an important regulator of vertebral trabecular bone mass and bone strength in adult mice (Nilsson et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nilsson et al., 2021

claim: RSPO3 could impact body fat distribution.
source: It was reported that RSPO3 could impact body fat distribution (Loh et al., 2020), and fat distribution is an independent predictor of type 2 diabetes (Manolopoulos et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Loh et al., 2020

claim: Fat distribution is an independent predictor of type 2 diabetes.
source: It was reported that RSPO3 could impact body fat distribution (Loh et al., 2020), and fat distribution is an independent predictor of type 2 diabetes (Manolopoulos et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Manolopoulos et al., 2010

claim: The use of insulin was reported to be associated with an increased risk of fracture.
source: For example, the use of insulin (Napoli et al., 2014) or thiazolidinediones (Zhu et al., 2014) was reported to be associated with an increased risk of fracture.
evidence: Supported by citation to Napoli et al., 2014

claim: The use of thiazolidinediones was reported to be associated with an increased risk of fracture.
source: For example, the use of insulin (Napoli et al., 2014) or thiazolidinediones (Zhu et al., 2014) was reported to be associated with an increased risk of fracture.
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhu et al., 2014

claim: The risk of falls was suggested to increase in the patients with T2D.
source: In addition, the risk of falls, which might be triggered by some diabetic complications such as visual impairment and peripheral neuropathy, was suggested to increase in the patients with T2D (Schwartz et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schwartz et al., 2002

claim: Low physical activity was identified as one of the most important independent diabetes-related risk factors for fracture through Gradient Boosting Machines.
source: Besides, low physical activity was identified as one of the most important independent diabetes-related risk factors for fracture through Gradient Boosting Machines (Axelsson et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Axelsson et al., 2023

claim: The observed effect size of type 2 diabetes on the risk of fracture decreased when the T2D-related risk factors decreased.
source: Therefore, in this study, we stratified the T2D patients with five risk factors (BMI ≤25 kg/m2, no physical activity, falls in the last year, HbA1c≥47.5 mmol/mol, and antidiabetic medication treatment), and found that the observed effect size of type 2 diabetes on the risk of fracture decreased when the T2D-related risk factors decreased, and the association became not significant if the type 2 diabetes patients carried none of the risk factors.
evidence: Supported by stratified Cox regression analysis in UK Biobank

claim: The association between T2D and fracture became not significant if the type 2 diabetes patients carried none of the risk factors.
source: Therefore, in this study, we stratified the T2D patients with five risk factors (BMI ≤25 kg/m2, no physical activity, falls in the last year, HbA1c≥47.5 mmol/mol, and antidiabetic medication treatment), and found that the observed effect size of type 2 diabetes on the risk of fracture decreased when the T2D-related risk factors decreased, and the association became not significant if the type 2 diabetes patients carried none of the risk factors.
evidence: Supported by stratified Cox regression analysis in UK Biobank

claim: The genetically determined T2D might not be associated with higher risk of fracture.
source: In conclusion, the genetically determined T2D might not be associated with higher risk of fracture.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from MR analyses

claim: The diabetic bone paradox might not exist if the T2D-related risk factors were eliminated.
source: Anyway, the diabetic bone paradox might not exist if the T2D-related risk factors were eliminated.
evidence: Inference drawn from stratified observational analyses

claim: It is important to manage the complications of T2D to prevent the risk of fracture.
source: Therefore, it is important to manage the complications of T2D to prevent the risk of fracture.
evidence: Recommendation based on study findings

claim: An intensive lifestyle intervention, such as weight loss, in T2D patients might increase fracture risk.
source: Our previous study suggested that keeping a moderate-high BMI (overweight) might be of benefit to old people in terms of fracture risk (Zhu et al., 2022), and an intensive lifestyle intervention, such as weight loss, in T2D patients might increase fracture risk (Johnson et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Johnson et al., 2017

claim: Hyperglycemia could cause osteocyte senescence and premature programmed cell death, leading to decreased ability to sense and respond to mechanical stimuli such as oscillatory shear stress, ultimately contributing to skeletal fragility.
source: The hyperglycemia could cause osteocyte senescence and premature programmed cell death, leading to decreased ability to sense and respond to mechanical stimuli such as oscillatory shear stress, ultimately contributing to skeletal fragility (Eckhardt et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Eckhardt et al., 2020

claim: Trabecular bone score and chest CT texture analysis could provide additional valuable information in the evaluation of fracture risk, especially in type 2 diabetes patients.
source: Other measurements, such as trabecular bone score (Fazullina et al., 2022; Ho-Pham and Nguyen, 2019) and chest CT texture analysis (Kim et al., 2023 ), could provide additional valuable information in the evaluation of fracture risk, especially in type 2 diabetes patients.
evidence: Supported by citations to Fazullina et al., 2022; Ho-Pham and Nguyen, 2019; Kim et al., 2023

claim: Mendelian randomization could be an alternative approach to infer the relationship between exposure and outcome, as this method exploits the idea that genotypes are distributed randomly at conception, facilitating their use as instrumental variables to alleviate the bias of the unknown confounding factors.
source: MR could be an alternative approach to infer the relationship between exposure and outcome, as this method exploits the idea that genotypes are distributed randomly at conception, facilitating their use as instrumental variables (IV) to alleviate the bias of the unknown confounding factors (Davey Smith and Hemani, 2014; Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Davey Smith and Hemani, 2014; Zhao et al., 2019

claim: Trajanoska et al., 2018 assessed the effect of 15 selected clinical risk factors on the risk of fracture by using two-sample MR analysis, and reported a non-significant relationship between type 2 diabetes and fracture risk, but the direction of effect was negative (OR = 0.99).
source: (Trajanoska et al., 2018) assessed the effect of 15 selected clinical risk factors on the risk of fracture by using two-sample MR analysis, and reported a non-significant relationship between type 2 diabetes and fracture risk, but the direction of effect was negative (OR = 0.99).
evidence: Supported by citation to Trajanoska et al., 2018

claim: The genetically predicted type 2 diabetes was associated with higher BMD, consistent with previous studies.
source: Furthermore, consistent with previous studies (Ahmad et al., 2017; Mitchell et al., 2021), the MR analysis in the present study suggested that the genetically predicted type 2 diabetes was associated with higher BMD.
evidence: Supported by citations to Ahmad et al., 2017; Mitchell et al., 2021, and current study data

claim: By alleviating the bias of the unknown confounding factors through MR analysis, the genetically predicted type 2 diabetes did not show the bone paradox.
source: That is to say, by alleviating the bias of the unknown confounding factors through MR analysis, the genetically predicted type 2 diabetes did not show this bone paradox.
evidence: Inference drawn from MR analysis results

claim: The different roles of the shared genetic components between bone metabolism and type 2 diabetes might provide one possible explanation for the inverse association pattern.
source: Therefore, we speculated that the different roles of the shared genetic components between bone metabolism and type 2 diabetes might provide one possible explanation for the inverse association pattern, and obese tendency might mediate this pattern.
evidence: Speculation based on genetic findings

claim: Obese tendency might mediate the inverse association pattern between bone metabolism and type 2 diabetes.
source: Therefore, we speculated that the different roles of the shared genetic components between bone metabolism and type 2 diabetes might provide one possible explanation for the inverse association pattern, and obese tendency might mediate this pattern.
evidence: Speculation based on genetic findings and mediation analysis

claim: In UK Biobank, the participants with type 2 diabetes had a higher BMI compared to those without diabetes (31.74 vs 27.05, p<2.2 × 10−16).
source: In fact, in UK Biobank, the participants with type 2 diabetes had a higher BMI compared to those without diabetes (31.74 vs 27.05, p<2.2 × 10−16), and BMI mediated 30.2% of the intermediary effect between type 2 diabetes and fracture in our study.
evidence: Supported by UK Biobank observational data

claim: Four factors (duration of T2D, low physical activity, BMI, and insulin treatment) were identified as the important risk factors for fracture among the T2D patients in a recent large-scale cohort study.
source: In a recent large-scale cohort study, four factors (duration of T2D, low physical activity, BMI, and insulin treatment) were identified as the important risk factors for fracture among the T2D patients, and the patients without the risk factors had lower fracture risk than their matched controls (Axelsson et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Axelsson et al., 2023

claim: T2D patients without risk factors had lower fracture risk than their matched controls.
source: In a recent large-scale cohort study, four factors (duration of T2D, low physical activity, BMI, and insulin treatment) were identified as the important risk factors for fracture among the T2D patients, and the patients without the risk factors had lower fracture risk than their matched controls (Axelsson et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Axelsson et al., 2023

claim: Significantly lower fracture risk was observed for overweight individuals (BMI 25–30 kg/m2) in type 2 diabetes than their counterparts without type 2 diabetes.
source: One previous study using the UK primary care data found no evidence to suggest a higher risk of fracture in type 2 diabetes patients (Davie et al., 2021) and reported that significantly lower fracture risk was observed for overweight individuals (BMI 25–30 kg/m2) in type 2 diabetes than their counterparts without type 2 diabetes (Davie et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Davie et al., 2021
